title: True, False or Not Given: 4 rules that stop guessing

tips.title: Treat each statement as a claim
tips.body: Read the statement and ask one question: does the passage agree, disagree or say nothing? Underline the key idea — a number, a comparison, a cause — because that is what you are checking.

tips.title: Find the matching sentence
tips.body: The statements follow the order of the passage. Scan for names, dates or unusual words, then read the sentence around them slowly. The answer is almost never spread across several paragraphs.

tips.title: False means the opposite
tips.body: Choose False only when the passage clearly contradicts the statement: “rose” versus “fell”, “all” versus “some”, “before” versus “after”. A missing detail is not a contradiction.

tips.title: Not Given means silent
tips.body: If the passage mentions the topic but not the specific claim, the answer is Not Given. Never fill the gap with general knowledge, however obvious the fact seems.

title: Matching headings: find the main idea fast

tips.title: Read the headings first
tips.body: Skim the list of headings before the passage and note how they differ. Two headings often share a word, so decide what makes each one unique.

tips.title: Skim for the paragraph’s purpose
tips.body: Read the first and last sentences of each paragraph and ask what the writer is doing: describing a problem, comparing, giving a solution or predicting. That purpose is the heading.

tips.title: Ignore matching single words
tips.body: A heading that repeats a word from the paragraph is often a trap. The right heading summarises the whole paragraph, not one example inside it.

tips.title: Do the easy ones first
tips.body: Answer the paragraphs you are sure about, cross those headings off, then return to the harder ones with fewer options left.

title: Summary and gap completion: 4 checks for full marks

tips.title: Check the word limit
tips.body: “NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS” means one or two words only. Numbers written as figures count as one word. Going over the limit scores zero, even if the idea is right.

tips.title: Predict the word type
tips.body: Look at the words around each gap. After “a” or “the” you need a noun; after “is very” you need an adjective. Predicting the grammar halves your search.

tips.title: Locate the section
tips.body: Summaries usually cover one part of the passage. Find where the first gap’s idea appears and stay in that section — the answers follow the text in order.

tips.title: Copy the exact spelling
tips.body: Take the words directly from the passage and copy them letter for letter. Check singular and plural so the completed sentence is grammatical.

title: Multiple choice: rule out the distractors

tips.title: Read the stem carefully
tips.body: The question stem tells you exactly what to find — a reason, a purpose, an opinion. Underline it before you look at the options.

tips.title: Find the evidence first
tips.body: Locate the answer in the passage before reading the options closely. Forming your own answer first makes it harder for a distractor to tempt you.

tips.title: Eliminate, then choose
tips.body: Wrong options are often true but do not answer the question, or use the passage’s words with a changed meaning. Cross out each option you can disprove.

tips.title: Watch for extreme words
tips.body: Options with “always”, “never” or “only” are right only if the passage is equally strong. Cautious language like “may” or “some” usually needs a cautious answer.
